newsitem.title: CANADA: Liberal majority seen boosting Canada dollar.
newsitem.headline: Liberal majority seen boosting Canada dollar.

text.p: The re-election of a Liberal majority government, coupled with a collapse by the separatist Bloc Quebecois in Canada's June 2 general election, would help boost the Canadian dollar, economists said on Tuesday.

"The best-case scenario if you're holding Canadian dollars is a Liberal majority government with some decent support from the other parties and a very dismal showing by the Bloc Quebecois," said Rick Egleton, deputy chief economist with Bank of Montreal.
A Reuters-Zogby national poll released on Monday showed the Liberals preferred by 47.6 percent of decided voters, with a commanding 31 point lead over their nearest rival, the Conservatives.
Analysts said the numbers comforted markets, which have grown accustomed to the cautious fiscal policies of the Liberal government.
"The markets know what to expect from a Liberal majority with Paul Martin back as finance minister because there is a track record there," Egleton said.
Since the election was called on April 30, the dollar has jumped 1.5 percent against the U.S. dollar, and is now worth 72.61 cents, up from 71.53 cents.
Market hunger for good news out of Quebec was fuelled as the pro-sovereignty Bloc Quebecois stumbled in its first week of campaigning.
The Bloc, the official opposition in the last parliament, was embarrassed after the party's chartered bus got lost last Friday en route to a campaign event in Quebec's Eastern Townships.
The widely reported mishap led to the replacement of the party's campaign manager and an acknowledgment by its leaders that the Bloc was spinning its electoral wheels.

"The markets are definitely taking notice. Our customers mention the Bloc because they are looking ahead to the next referendum," said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Toronto-based Lehman Brothers.
There was speculation that a weak performance by the Bloc could disrupt the timetable for the next Quebec referendum by Quebec's separatist government and lead to a rally in the Canadian dollar.
Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard, the founder of the Bloc Quebecois, is expected to call a provincial election in 1998, followed possibly by a snap sovereignty referendum.

"Fewer Bloc seats would be seen as a setback for the sovereignty movement and it would give the market even more reasons to be bullish on the currency," said Rob Palombi, economist with MMS International.
But hopes that the Canadian dollar -- which sank to a two-year low in April -- would soar after the June 2 ballot could be wishful thinking, some analysts said.

"There is some evidence of significant depreciation of the Canadian dollar immediately following a federal election," said Gregory, who has tracked currency fluctuations during the seven federal elections held since 1970.
There has tended to be a buy on rumour, sell on fact tendency with speculators selling the dollar after an election, Gregory said.
But there was a consensus that a minority government in which no party held a majority of parliamentary seats, was the wild card for the Canadian dollar.
Canada's last minority government was that of Conservative Joe Clark, which survived less than a year in office in 1979-80.

"It would be unambiguously negative," Gregory said. "Even if the balance of power is held by right-wing parties, you know that you have to go back to the people in a year or two, which unfortunately would coincide with a Quebec election.
"The markets would read a lot of Quebec risk into that kind of situation," Gregory added.
